title: Input Staging vs Token Emit: Pipeline Scheduling & Stream Tiering (notes, sim results)
body:
Purpose:
This doc scribbles through a different framing for the classic prefill vs decode problem: treat the two phases as "input staging" (what we usually call prefill / kv population) and "token emission" (decode/streaming). Goal is to find scheduler primitives and stream-tiering rules that let us:
- overlap input-stage work with low-latency token emission for other streams,
- maximize GPU kernel utilization (longer microbatches when ok, but preserve tail-latency SLOs),
- bound KV cache memory pressure and coherence costs, and
- expose a small set of knobs to upper layers (console / routing) for predictable cost tradeoffs.

Summary of the idea (high level):
1) Classify live requests into three run-time tiers: "interactive-high" (latency-sensitive, token-by-token streaming), "bulk-prep" (long input-stage, can accept a few hundred ms of jitter), and "elastic" (background/batch).
2) Maintain two scheduling lanes on the GPU: an emission lane and a staging lane.
   - Emission lane: optimized for low-latency kernel paths (small batch sizes, prefer fused-kernels with small-seq optimizations).
   - Staging lane: optimized for throughput (large microbatches, sequence packing, attention kernel selection targeting long sequences).
3) Allow controlled handoffs: when staging finishes a chunk of KV entries for a request, the request becomes eligible for emission. If the emission lane is congested, a short in-GPU buffer (per-stream KV slice) can hold most-recent prefixes to reduce round-trip to CPU.

Why this framing?
- We want to avoid the binary "prefill first, then decode" model that forces long-lived prefill on the critical path.
- By treating staging as a first-class streaming workload, we can schedule it against emission with explicit priorities rather than implicit stall-yielding.

Constraints & background we must respect:
- Some kernels (esp quantized ones) have large startup costs; microbatching improves throughput dramatically but hurts per-request latency.
- KV cache size is bounded: we must maintain a per-GPU working set and evict / remote-page as needed.
- Model variants exist: some models support faster attention paths for short decode steps; scheduler must pick kernel variants per-lane.

Core scheduler primitives (proposal):
- lane_assign(stream_id, request_meta) -> lane_id (emission | staging | elastic)
- stage_enqueue(request_chunk) -> adds to staging microbatch queue
- emit_enqueue(request_token_event) -> low-latency queue for token emission
- fast_yield_check(epoch) -> preemptive check executed at kernel boundaries to allow emission lane to take priority
- kv_reserve(stream_id, bytes) -> pessimistic reservation for staging to avoid eviction thrash
- kv_commit(stream_id, prefix_range) -> marks that prefix keys are now resident and safe to use by emission lane

Microbatching math (toy model used in local sim):
- staging throughput T_s ~ f(batch_size, seq_len_avg) with diminishing returns beyond 64-128 microbatch size for our fused attention kernel.
- emission latency L_e ~ base_kernel_ms + per_token_ms * (1 / effective_batching_factor). For interactive streams we keep effective_batching_factor <= 8.
- cost per token is minimized when staging batch_size is large and emission batch_factor is > 16, but interactive SLOs force smaller factors.

Simulator experiments (quick notes):
- ran a discrete-event sim with synthetic mix: 60% interactive-high, 30% bulk-prep, 10% elastic. Seq lengths: interactive 8-64, prep 512-2048.
- naive all-prefill-first baseline: tail P95 latency for interactive streams = 420ms, GPU utilization 42%
- separate-lanes with strict priority (emission always preempt staging): P95 interactive = 42ms, GPU util = 61% (staging suffers)
- adaptive backoff policy (staging yields only if emission queue depth > 4 or emission waiting-time > 15ms): P95 interactive = 48ms, GPU util = 74%
- with small per-stream in-GPU prefix buffer (config: 64KB/stream, ring buffer): P95 interactive = 50ms, GPU util = 78% and staging completion latency improves 15% vs strict priority because fewer preemptions required.

KV cache coherence & memory management:
- We observed that frequent KV writes from staging interleaved with emission reads cause hotspots and occasional evictions of large prefix blocks.
- Proposal: implement a two-tier KV residency model: 
  * committed region: contiguous KV slices that are fully populated and pinned until request completes or eviction policy triggers; written by staging -> commit.
  * transient write-buffer: small append-only region used during staging microbatch; can be evicted cheaply since emission should wait on commit to read beyond its current prefix.
- Eviction policy change: prefer evicting transient buffers first, and prefer evicting largest idle requests (elastic) before active interactive streams.
- Small in-GPU slab allocation for hot prefixes: populate and pin small slices (configurable) to reduce CPU-GPU round trips.

Kernel selection heuristics (how scheduler chooses kernels for lanes):
- Emission lane: prefer small-sequence optimized kernels (attention tiling tuned for seq<=64), enable fused-softmax-kernel when supported, use 8-bit kernels only if accuracy tests for short-step decode pass.
- Staging lane: prefer large-seq kernels, attention cache-friendly variants, and allow autotune to pick larger block sizes.
- If both lanes can use the same kernel with different launch params, try to coalesce small emission launches into a single grouped kernel launch when emission queue accumulates slightly (within SLO window).

Operational knobs to surface (API / Console):
- stream_priority: {interactive-high, interactive-standard, prep, batch}
- kv_pin_budget: bytes reserved for interactive streams on a per-GPU basis
- staging_yield_thresholds: {queue_depth, waiting_ms}
- microbatch_target: desired microbatch size for staging lane (auto if 0)
- emission_max_batch_factor: cap used to restrict how much emission can batch tokens to gain throughput vs latency

Open questions & tradeoffs (TODOs / discussion points):
- How big should the in-GPU prefix buffer be to justify memory fragmentation risk? 32KB vs 64KB vs 128KB tradeoffs need real mem traces.
- Can we reuse streaming RPC semantics to mark "committed prefix" boundaries to avoid full kv_commit call? This would save a round-trip but complicate consistency guarantees.
- Is it worth a hybrid kernel that does partial KV writes during emission for extremely tight latency budgets? Risk: interleaving writes could cause stalls for long-seq staging kernels.
- Autoscaling interaction: staging-heavy workloads could trigger scale-up; should we bias routing to dedicated staging-only pools for customers that do long input pipelines?
- Fault scenarios: what if a staging microbatch fails mid-run and some committed slices are missing? Need idempotent commit semantics and a quick fallback that lets emission continue up to last good prefix.

Short-term engineering plan (next 6 weeks):
W1: add sim metric hooks to existing simulator (GH: redwood/serving-simulator#178). Collect mem traces by workload shape from prod traces.
W2: prototype lane scheduler in runtime shim: 2 queues, preemption callback, simple kv_reserve/commit. Limited to single-GPU dev node.
W3: run A/B between strict-priority and adaptive-backoff policies on dev cluster with TTL-limited traffic replay.
W4: add in-GPU prefix buffer prototype and run microbenchmarks for fragment+evict scenarios.
W5: define console knobs and telemetry events: lane_assignments, preempt_count, kv_eviction_reasons.

How this differs from prior notes:
- this doc intentionally avoids naming "prefill" and "decode" as a serial handoff; treats both as streaming workloads that can be scheduled concurrently with explicit priority rules and a small in-GPU buffer to reduce round-trips.
- emphasis on simple primitives (kv_reserve/commit) rather than full transactional KV semantics.

Actionable immediate tasks for collaborators:
- Ethan: add mem traces + realistic prefix sizes from ops (JIRA INF-3207).
- Priya: sketch UI knobs for per-customer kv_pin_budget and a visualization for preempt_count in console.
- Liam: add kernel variant flags to runtime launch logic so scheduler can pick short-seq vs long-seq kernels at runtime.

Notes to self / rough thoughts:
- If we can get 70-80% GPU utilization while keeping P95 interactive < 60ms we win a lot of unit-cost arguments.
- Be careful: some customers will prefer deterministic latency even at cost of lower utilization; keep lane policy per-tenant.
- Add a mode where staging runs on separate dedicated GPUs to simplify scheduling - but this reduces the unified runtime promise; still useful as enterprise option.

References & links to related threads (copy-paste):
- Slack: #serving-runtime: "input-staging lane idea" (thread ts 1678823345.001200)
- GH: redwood/serving-simulator#178 - where sim harness lives
- JIRA: INF-3421 - prototype lane scheduler

Unresolved: prioritization fairness across tenants. If one tenant sends many interactive streams, how do we avoid starvation of other tenants' staging? Consider tenant-weighted credits per GPU.

End of notes.
